## INTRO

Imagine opening the results of your annual blood test. You feel fine, you have been walking more, and you recently started working with light weights to stay strong. But one number on the report is higher than before: creatinine. Then you remember the creatine powder sitting beside your coffee maker. Could the supplement be hurting your kidneys?

Creatine and creatinine sound almost identical, but they are not the same thing. And a change in a blood test is not always the same as a change in kidney health. Today we will separate those ideas, look at what research actually tells us, and explain which questions are worth asking before you use a supplement. Especially if you are over fifty, or already have kidney concerns.

## CH1

First, why are people talking about creatine at all? Creatine is a substance your body naturally makes. You also get some from foods such as fish and meat. Inside muscles, it helps replenish energy during brief, demanding efforts. Think about standing from a low chair, climbing a flight of stairs, or completing a careful set of strength exercises. Those movements are different from a long, easy walk. They ask your muscles for bursts of effort.

As we get older, preserving strength becomes an important part of daily independence. Research in older adults suggests that adding creatine to resistance training may provide a modest extra improvement in muscle strength. But the findings are less certain for improvements in everyday physical function or muscle size. Creatine is not a substitute for movement, adequate nutrition, sleep, or a training plan suited to your abilities. Nor does being over fifty automatically mean you need it.

Here is the practical distinction. Getting creatine through a normal meal is not the same decision as starting a concentrated supplement every day. Food brings many nutrients with it. A supplement adds a particular substance in a measured amount, and it belongs on the list of things you tell your healthcare team you take. That distinction matters even more once we look at your lab results.
